750.title: Good Friday
750.hook: Christians remember the crucifixion, often in silence
750.howItsDone: On Good Friday, Christians gather to hear the passion read, pray at the cross, and keep the day quietly; Catholics have no Mass that day, and Orthodox Christians sing laments around the epitaphios, the image of Christ in the tomb.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a city sitting alone like a widow, read low on the ninth of Av. Your line was how lonely sits the city. Did one verse find you? Today, another day kept for grief. Day seven hundred fifty.

Something is missing from the church this afternoon. The altar is bare. No flowers. In some churches the bells stay silent, and people come in without chatting and leave without a word. A wooden cross may be carried in, and one by one people walk up to it. It's the Friday before Easter, the day Christians remember the death of Jesus. And its name, oddly, is Good Friday. Today: what is remembered, and why so much of the remembering happens in silence.
screen: `A BARE ALTAR.` → `PEOPLE LEAVE WITHOUT A WORD.` → `WHY CALL IT GOOD?`

segments.voice: First, the darkness. The Gospels tell how Jesus was crucified under the Roman governor, Pontius Pilate, outside Jerusalem. Matthew writes, "Now from the sixth hour there was darkness over all the land unto the ninth hour." The day goes dark in the middle. Second, the cry. Matthew records Jesus calling out, "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" They are the opening words of Psalm 22, a lament. On the cross, he prays an old prayer of abandonment. Christians sit with that line: the one they call God's Son, voicing the feeling of being left alone. Third, different words from different Gospels. Luke gives a quieter last word: "Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit." John gives this: "It is finished." The Bible doesn't choose between them. It keeps all three side by side: the cry, the trust, the ending. Fourth, the silence. In Christian belief, Easter is coming, but the day's customs don't rush to it. Catholic churches celebrate no Mass on Good Friday; instead there is a service of the Lord's Passion and the veneration of the cross. Orthodox Christians gather around an embroidered image of Christ's body laid in the tomb and sing laments. Some Protestant churches hold services of readings and long pauses, some ending in darkness. Why good? Christian teaching answers with what it holds that death opened: forgiveness, and the way to Easter. But the day itself is kept quiet, the way you stay with someone who has died before you talk about anything else.
screen: `DARKNESS FROM THE SIXTH HOUR.` · `MY GOD, WHY HAST THOU FORSAKEN ME?` · `INTO THY HANDS; IT IS FINISHED.` · `NO RUSH TO EASTER.` · then, large: `A QUIET HOUR.`

segments.voice: For these two minutes, begin a quiet hour. Put the phone face down, or across the room. Let the sounds around you be the only sounds. If a thought pulls at you, notice it and let the quiet return. You don't need to think about the cross unless you want to. You can simply practice the thing the day teaches: staying with something hard without rushing to the next thing. If you pray, you can pray with the words from Luke, into thy hands. The bell holds the time.
Good Friday: the day Christians remember the crucifixion of Jesus, kept with bare altars, readings and silence before Easter. Today's word.
Your line: a quiet hour. Today, keep one hour quiet: no screens, no background noise, just the hour. Day seven hundred fifty.

751.title: Ashura, remembered grief
751.hook: Shia Muslims mourn Husayn's death at Karbala; Sunni Muslims fast this day recalling Moses' rescue
751.howItsDone: On Ashura, Shia Muslims gather at majalis to hear the story of Karbala retold, recite laments, and join processions in mourning for Husayn; Sunni Muslims fast the day, following the hadith about Moses' rescue, and some fast the day before as well.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a bare altar and a cry from Psalm 22. Your line was a quiet hour. Did you find one, and what filled it? Today, one day on the Muslim calendar, remembered in two ways. Day seven hundred fifty-one.

Two homes, the same morning. In the first, a family dresses in black. Tonight they'll go to a gathering where a reciter tells an old story, slowly, in a voice that breaks, and people in the room weep with him. In the second home, someone skips breakfast and lunch, fasting, and breaks the fast at sunset with dates and water. Both households are Muslim. Both are keeping the same day, the tenth of the month of Muharram. Its name is Ashura.
screen: `ONE FAMILY IN BLACK.` → `ANOTHER, FASTING TILL SUNSET.` → `THE SAME DAY: ASHURA.`

segments.voice: First, the rescue. A report in the hadith collection of al-Bukhari says that when the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, came to Medina, he found the Jews of the city fasting on this day. They told him it was the day God saved the Children of Israel from their enemy, and that Moses had fasted on it. The Prophet said Muslims had a claim on Moses too, and he fasted the day and told others to fast. So in Sunni tradition, Ashura is a day of fasting and thanks for Moses' rescue. Second, the grief. Shia tradition remembers Husayn, the son of Ali and Fatima, the Prophet's grandson. Tradition tells how he set out with his family and a small band of companions, refused to give his allegiance to the ruler Yazid, and was surrounded on the plain of Karbala, in what is now Iraq. The story says they were cut off from the river and suffered thirst. On Ashura, Husayn and those with him were killed. Third, remembered grief. In Shia communities the story is retold every year at gatherings called majalis. People weep, recite poems of lament, and walk in processions. The grief is kept on purpose. In Shia tradition, mourning Husayn is an act of loyalty to him, and his stand is remembered as a stand against injustice. Fourth, two remembrances, side by side. Sunni tradition also honors Husayn as the Prophet's grandson, and Shia tradition also tells of the rescue of Moses. The day holds both. Grief that is remembered on a set day, in company, doesn't fade into silence.
screen: `A FAST FOR MOSES' RESCUE.` · `HUSAYN AT KARBALA.` · `GRIEF KEPT ON PURPOSE.` · `ONE DAY, TWO REMEMBRANCES.` · then, large: `REMEMBERED GRIEF.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath settle. Choose one thing you learned about Karbala today: a small band of companions, a river cut off, a grandson who would not give his allegiance. Hold that one fact, gently, as you would hold a name at a memorial. Then let a grief of your own come near, if one is there. Don't push it away, and don't dig. Just let it be remembered, here, for a few breaths, in company with a much older grief. The bell holds the time.
Ashura: the tenth of Muharram, a fast for Moses' rescue, and the day Shia Muslims mourn Husayn at Karbala. Today's word.
Your line: remembered grief. Today, learn one more fact about Karbala from a Shia source, and say it to someone. Day seven hundred fifty-one.

what it means: one day, two remembrances: a fast for Moses' rescue, and mourning for Husayn at Karbala.
what a scholar hears: Sahih al-Bukhari 2004 on the fast; the Karbala narrative at the heart of Shia mourning gatherings (majalis).

752.title: Holocaust Remembrance Day
752.hook: on the anniversary of the liberation of Auschwitz, the world remembers the Jews murdered in the Holocaust and all the Nazis' victims
752.howItsDone: On Holocaust remembrance days, communities, schools and governments hold ceremonies where names of victims are read aloud, candles are lit, and survivors' testimonies are heard; Jewish communities also keep Yom HaShoah in the spring.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ashura: a fast for Moses' rescue, and mourning for Husayn at Karbala. Your line was remembered grief. What did you learn, and who did you tell? Today, a day of remembering in our own time. Day seven hundred fifty-two.

Someone steps up to a microphone with a printed list and reads a name. A first name, a family name, a town. Then the next person reads another. Nobody makes a speech. Nobody explains. The names keep coming, one voice after another, and the room just listens. Ceremonies like this happen on days set aside to remember the Holocaust: the murder of Europe's Jews by Nazi Germany and its collaborators, and the murder of many others alongside them. Today is about why a single name matters so much there.
screen: `A PRINTED LIST.` → `ONE NAME, THEN ANOTHER.` → `NOBODY MAKES A SPEECH.`

segments.voice: First, the day. In a resolution, the United Nations General Assembly set an international day of remembrance on the anniversary of the liberation of Auschwitz, in January. It remembers the Jews who were murdered, along with members of other minorities. Among the Nazis' other victims were Roma and disabled people. Israel and Jewish communities also keep their own day of remembrance, Yom HaShoah, in the spring. Second, a place and a name. The Holocaust memorial in Jerusalem is called Yad Vashem, words taken from the book of Isaiah. In the King James Bible, God promises people who feared they would leave nothing behind: "Even unto them will I give in mine house and within my walls a place and a name better than of sons and of daughters: I will give them an everlasting name, that shall not be cut off." A place, and a name, that shall not be cut off. Third, why names. The scale of the Holocaust is so vast that the mind can go blank before it, the way it can go numb before distant suffering, as we heard a few days ago. A name undoes that. A name had a kitchen, a street, a favorite song, someone who called it at dinnertime. Reading one name turns a number back into a person. Fourth, remembering as a duty. Some survivors spoke and wrote so that what happened would not be forgotten or denied. Remembering here is not dwelling. It is keeping faith with people who were meant to vanish without a trace, and keeping watch over the present, so that hatred is recognized early.
screen: `A DAY THE WORLD SET ASIDE.` · `A PLACE AND A NAME.` · `A NAME TURNS A NUMBER INTO A PERSON.` · `KEEPING FAITH WITH THE MURDERED.` · then, large: `REMEMBER.`

segments.voice: If you can do it safely, light a candle. If not, picture one. Sit with the flame for a few breaths. Later today, find one name of someone murdered in the Holocaust; memorials keep online lists of names and stories for exactly this. For now, sit quietly, and let the flame stand in for that person you haven't met yet. When you find the name, read it aloud once, slowly, with their town if it's given. If you pray, you can hold them in prayer. The bell holds the time.
Holocaust Remembrance Day: the international day, on the anniversary of the liberation of Auschwitz, for remembering the Holocaust's victims by name. Today's word.
Your line: remember. Today, light a candle, real or imagined, and read one name aloud. Day seven hundred fifty-two.

753.title: It can rise
753.hook: Seneca on the burned city of Lyon: cities, and people, can rise again (Letters 91)
753.howItsDone: Some readers of the Stoics turn to Seneca's letters in hard seasons, using his practice of rehearsing possible losses in advance, and his reminder that what falls can be rebuilt.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a list of names read aloud, and a place and a name that shall not be cut off. Your line was remember. Whose name did you read? Today, after the days of mourning, a letter about rebuilding. Day seven hundred fifty-three.

Word arrives from far away, and there is nothing anyone can do but read it. A city in Gaul, the colony the Romans called Lugdunum, the place we call Lyon, has burned. A man named Liberalis, who has ties to the city, is crushed. His friend Seneca, the Stoic writer, hears about it, and sits down to write a letter to another friend, Lucilius. It begins with Liberalis's grief, and it doesn't wave it away.
screen: `A CITY IN GAUL HAS BURNED.` → `LIBERALIS IS CRUSHED.` → `SENECA PICKS UP A PEN.`

segments.voice: First, one night. Seneca is struck by how fast it happened. In his telling, a single night stood between a great city and no city at all. Everything a city builds slowly, a fire can take quickly. He doesn't pretend otherwise. Second, expect it. Seneca's advice is an old Stoic one: let the mind rehearse what could happen, so that loss, when it comes, doesn't come as a total stranger. Nothing, he says, should be unexpected by us. That can sound cold. In the letter it reads more like a friend saying: we live in a world where things fall, and you are allowed to know that ahead of time. Third, it can rise. Here the letter turns. Seneca reminds Lucilius that cities have been leveled before, by fire and by earthquake, and have been raised again, and that the ruin can make room for something better. He hopes the same for Lyon. Not the same city. A city, rising. Fourth, people too. The letter moves on from the city to human lives, to bodies and their endings. Some readers carry his turn over to a person: what falls in a life can sometimes be rebuilt, slowly, stone by stone. This is not a promise that every loss gets fixed. Yesterday we read names that can never be given their lives back, and grief like that doesn't need a happy ending. Seneca's point is narrower. Ruin is real, and so is rebuilding. Both belong to the world. Today, after days of mourning, the second half gets its turn.
screen: `ONE NIGHT BETWEEN A CITY AND NONE.` · `LET NOTHING COME AS A STRANGER.` · `CITIES HAVE RISEN AGAIN.` · `PEOPLE, TOO, STONE BY STONE.` · then, large: `IT CAN RISE.`

segments.voice: Sit easily. Bring to mind one small thing in your life that has fallen down: a habit you dropped, a shelf that collapsed, a friendship gone quiet, a garden left to weeds. Not the biggest ruin. A small one. Look at it honestly, as Seneca looks at Lyon. Then picture the first stone going back. One text. One drawer sorted. One seed in the ground. Just the first stone, nothing more. Breathe with that picture. After the bell, go and set it. The bell holds the time.
It can rise: Seneca's letter about a grieving friend, and the hope that what has fallen can be built again. Today's word.
Your line: it can rise. Today, rebuild one small thing, and let it be only the first stone. Day seven hundred fifty-three.

754.title: Your map of suffering
754.hook: which teachings and practices actually help you?
754.howItsDone: Some people keep a written list of what helps in hard times, from scripture verses and prayers to walks and phone numbers, and some therapists and chaplains help people draw up such a plan before a crisis.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Seneca's letter about a city burned in one night. Your line was it can rise. What first stone did you set? Today, we start to close the question of suffering, with a pencil. Day seven hundred fifty-four.

An old trail map, folded and refolded until the creases have gone soft. Someone has written on it in pencil. A circle around a spring: good water. An X on a shortcut: don't, it floods. A star on a ledge: sat here, saw everything. The printed map shows the whole mountain. The pencil shows what one walker learned on it. For weeks now this path has been walking through suffering, with teachings from many traditions. Today, the pencil comes out.
screen: `A MAP WITH PENCIL MARKS.` → `GOOD WATER. DON'T, IT FLOODS.` → `TODAY, THE PENCIL COMES OUT.`

segments.voice: First, a map, not a creed. A creed says what is true for everyone. A map of suffering says something smaller and more useful: what has actually helped this one person, on this one road. It doesn't have to settle why suffering exists. It only has to mark the springs and the floods. Second, look back at what we've walked. The Buddha's teaching of the second arrow: the pain, and then the pain we add to it. The psalmist's question, how long, said straight to God. Patience, sabr, in the Qur'an. The friends who sat with Job in silence, before they ruined it by talking. Viktor Frankl's last freedom, the choice of an attitude. These last two weeks: a small mercy, a quiet hour, one day at a time, a city rising. Each came from its own tradition, and each stays with its own source. Your map can hold several without blending them into one teaching. Third, two columns. On one side, what helps. On the other, what doesn't, even when it's supposed to. Some people find advice makes things worse, and silence helps. Some find a practice that works on a bad day and fails on a terrible one. Both are worth writing down. An honest map has X marks too. Fourth, maps change. A map drawn young looks different later on. A teaching that meant nothing last year may be the spring you need next year. So the map stays in pencil. Write it today, and expect to erase.
screen: `A MAP, NOT A CREED.` · `WHAT WE'VE WALKED, EACH IN ITS PLACE.` · `WHAT HELPS, WHAT DOESN'T.` · `KEEP IT IN PENCIL.` · then, large: `WHAT HELPS ME.`

segments.voice: Take a piece of paper, or a note on your phone. Draw a line down the middle. On the left, write what helps when things are hard: a teaching, a practice, a person, a place, a song. On the right, what doesn't help, even if it's meant to. Don't think too long. Three on each side is plenty. Then sit quietly and look at the left column. Notice which one you'd reach for first. If you pray, prayer may be on your map; it belongs there if it helps. The bell holds the time.
Your map of suffering: a pencil map, in two columns, of the teachings and practices that actually help you, each kept with its source. Today's word.
Your line: what helps me. Today, keep the map somewhere you'll find it on a bad day, and add one mark before bed. Day seven hundred fifty-four.

755.title: To your past self
755.hook: write to the you who suffered most
755.howItsDone: Some people write letters to their younger selves in journals, in therapy, or on anniversaries of a hard time, offering the company they didn't have then rather than advice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a pencil map in two columns, the springs and the floods. Your line was what helps me. What mark did you add before bed? Today, a letter that goes backward in time. Day seven hundred fifty-five.

Seven battered ships have been dragged up on a beach nobody recognizes. Men soaked and shaking, the rest of the fleet scattered by the storm. This is the opening of Virgil's Aeneid, the Roman epic. The hero, Aeneas, has to say something to his men. He has no good news. He doesn't know where they are or whether the others are alive. So he says something strange: a sentence aimed at a future none of them can see yet.
screen: `SEVEN SHIPS ON A STRANGE BEACH.` → `NO GOOD NEWS TO GIVE.` → `A SENTENCE AIMED AT THE FUTURE.`

segments.voice: First, the line. In Latin, forsan et haec olim meminisse iuvabit. Put plainly: perhaps one day it will help to remember even this. Not that it's fine. Not that it happened for a reason. Only that someday, looking back, remembering this hour may bring something like gladness. The man who survives it will see it differently than the man inside it. Second, what Aeneas hides. Virgil adds a detail right after the speech. Aeneas wears hope on his face, and presses his grief down deep in his heart. He is sick at heart with huge cares of his own. The future self he points to is also the self he needs. Third, turn it around. Aeneas spoke from inside the storm toward a future he couldn't see. Today, you may be the one standing on the far side, looking back. Somewhere behind you is the version of you who had the hardest time: a year, a night, a hospital corridor, a move, a loss. That person couldn't know that you would be sitting here, on day seven hundred fifty-five of a practice, breathing. You can know it. Fourth, what to write. Not advice; that person has heard enough advice, and a couple of weeks ago we saw presence come before solutions. Not a lecture about what they should have done. Something closer to Aeneas: company, and a report from the future. Three lines is enough. Some people find words like: I see you. It was as hard as it felt. You made it here.
screen: `PERHAPS ONE DAY IT WILL HELP TO REMEMBER.` · `HOPE ON HIS FACE, GRIEF IN HIS HEART.` · `NOW YOU STAND ON THE FAR SIDE.` · `COMPANY, NOT ADVICE.` · then, large: `YOU MADE IT HERE.`

segments.voice: Find paper, or open a note. Close your eyes for a breath and let the you who suffered most come to mind. Just notice how old they were, and where. Don't relive it; just see them, from here. Then write three lines to them. Start with their name, or with dear me. Line one: what you see in them. Line two: something true about now. Line three, if it fits: you made it here. When you're done, put the pen down and sit with them for the rest of the time. The bell holds the time.
To your past self: three lines of company sent backward, to the you who suffered most, from the far side of it. Today's word.
Your line: you made it here. Today, keep the three lines somewhere private, and read them once more before you sleep. Day seven hundred fifty-five.

756.title: To someone suffering now
756.hook: a short note can matter more than it seems
756.howItsDone: People on different paths send cards, letters or messages to the sick and the grieving; Jewish, Christian and Muslim communities each have customs of visiting and writing to those in mourning.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Aeneas on a strange beach, and three lines sent back to the you who suffered most. Your line was you made it here. A week's end: a quiet hour, Ashura, remember, it can rise, a map, a letter backward. Today, a letter forward. Day seven hundred fifty-six.
screen: `YOU MADE IT HERE.` · `A WEEK OF DAYS KEPT FOR GRIEF.`

segments.voice: It's been on the fridge through two kitchens: a card held up by a magnet, the corners gone soft. It only says a few lines in a friend's handwriting. Nobody would call it literature. But the person who kept it can tell you exactly what week it arrived, and what that week was like. Yesterday's letter went backward, to someone who can't read it. Today's goes forward, to someone who can.
screen: `A CARD ON A FRIDGE.` → `A FEW LINES, KEPT FOR YEARS.` → `TODAY'S LETTER GOES FORWARD.`

segments.voice: First, letters as company. Seneca, whose letter about Lyon we read three days ago, wrote to his friend Lucilius about the letters they traded. A letter from an absent friend, he says, brings something real of that friend: a trace of the hand, a way of being present across a distance. It isn't the same as a visit. It isn't nothing. Second, comfort both ways. Paul's letter to the Romans opens with a man who can't be there yet. "For I long to see you," he writes, and then he says what he hopes for: "that I may be comforted together with you by the mutual faith both of you and me." Notice the word together. The writer isn't only handing comfort down from above; he expects some to come back. You don't have to share Paul's faith to recognize the shape. A note to someone suffering is one person reaching toward another across a distance, and either one may end up comforted. Third, keep it short. We've seen what Job's friends did once they started talking. A note to someone suffering doesn't explain, fix, or find the silver lining. It doesn't say everything happens for a reason. It says: I know. I'm thinking of you. I'm here. Fourth, the line. You're not alone. On the page it can look plain. In a hard week, from a real person, with their name at the bottom, it can be the thing someone keeps on the fridge. The note works because it's specific: their name, your name, one true sentence between them.
